messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette is missing some reported symptoms or demographic details. Rewrite it to include everything.

Previous vignette:
# Clinical Vignette: Priya

Priya was twenty-one when the shelling came to her neighbourhood in Lahore. She had been visiting her grandmother for the summer before starting her final year of university, a trip she had made every year since childhood. Her grandmother's house sat on a quiet street lined with neem trees, three blocks from the main road. On a Tuesday morning in July, while Priya was helping her grandmother prepare lunch, the first explosion rattled the windows so violently that a glass of water jumped from the kitchen counter and shattered on the tile floor. There was a moment of silence, then another blast—closer this time—and her grandmother grabbed her hand and pulled her toward the back room. Priya remembers this moment as a still image: her grandmother's face, the particular angle of afternoon light through the kitchen window, the feeling of her own hand being squeezed. Then another picture: crouching in the rear hallway, her grandmother's dupatta wrapped around both of them. Then nothing coherent—only fragments. A sound like breaking metal. The weight of her grandmother pressing against her. A smell she cannot name. A shape she saw but cannot quite hold in her mind, though it surfaces sometimes in her peripheral vision and makes her stomach clench. The shelling lasted perhaps twenty minutes, though Priya has no sense of time passing. When it stopped, there was dust in the air and a ringing in her ears that took hours to fade.

Now, two years later, Priya works as an auditor for a mid-sized firm in Chicago, where she moved to complete her degree and start her career. On the surface, her life appears orderly. She arrives at the office by eight-thirty, completes her spreadsheets with precision, and maintains cordial professional relationships with her colleagues. But something fundamental has shifted inside her, in a way she struggles to articulate even to herself. When she tries to explain to the intake clinician why she is here, the words scatter. She knows what happened—the event is not forgotten—but the experience itself feels locked behind glass. She can see it but cannot reach it, cannot translate it into language that makes sense. She has tried to write it down several times and abandoned the effort each time, frustrated and exhausted by the impossibility of finding the right words.

The triggers are specific and relentless. Two months ago, a colleague arrived at work on a bicycle, leaning it against the brick exterior of their building. When Priya saw the bicycle—the frame, the wheels, the way it stood upright in the morning sun—her heart began to race and she felt a sudden, overwhelming need to leave the office. She told her supervisor she was unwell and drove home, though she could not have explained why a bicycle frightened her. She knows, rationally, that bicycles have nothing to do with what happened. Yet the image of one is enough to send her into a state of hypervigilance that can last for hours. Similarly, any loud, percussive sound—a car backfiring, a door slamming, the sharp crack of a dropped file folder—sends her into immediate panic. She has begun to dread the commute to work, the unpredictability of urban noise, the sense that danger could announce itself at any moment.

What troubles her most is the feeling that she is no longer herself. The person she was before that summer—competent, engaged, capable of imagining a future—feels like someone she used to know but has lost contact with. She sits in meetings and performs the role of auditor, but the performance feels hollow. She goes through the motions of her job with technical proficiency, yet she experiences nothing while doing it. No satisfaction, no frustration, no sense of accomplishment. It is as though she is watching herself from outside her body, observing her own hands moving across the keyboard, her own mouth forming words in meetings, but feeling nothing from within. She has come to believe that she is fundamentally broken, that something essential was taken from her during those minutes in her grandmother's hallway and has not returned. She describes herself as feeling "dead inside"—not suicidal, not actively wishing for death, but experiencing a profound numbness that makes her question whether she is still a person at all or merely an object moving through space, performing human functions without any of the interior aliveness that should accompany them.

It was her mother who finally insisted she seek help. During a video call last month, her mother noticed that Priya's voice sounded flat, her responses mechanical. When pressed, Priya admitted that she had been avoiding leaving her apartment on weekends, that she had declined her firm's invitation to a team lunch, that she could not remember the last time she had felt anything like joy or even mild pleasure. What frightened her most was the possibility that this numbness was permanent, that she would spend the rest of her life as a shell—functional but fundamentally absent from her own existence.

Missing items that MUST appear in the rewrite:
MISSING FROM VIGNETTE:
- Snapshot Memory: Snapshot Memory is present: 'Priya remembers this moment as a still image' and 'Then another picture' directly reflect the snapshot memory symptom
- Incomplete Picture: Incomplete Picture is present: 'A shape she saw but cannot quite hold in her mind' and 'fragments' and 'only fragments' reflect incomplete/fragmented memory
- Cannot Find Words: Cannot Find Words is present: 'the words scatter' and 'she struggles to articulate' and 'the impossibility of finding the right words' and 'she could not have explained' directly address inability to verbalize
- No Longer Capable: No Longer Capable is present: 'The person she was before that summer—competent, engaged, capable of imagining a future—feels like someone she used to know but has lost contact with' reflects loss of capability and identity
- Dehumanization: Dehumanization is present: 'she is still a person at all or merely an object moving through space' and 'a shell—functional but fundamentally absent' reflect objectification and loss of personhood
- Emotional Numbness: Emotional Numbness is present: 'She describes herself as feeling dead inside' and 'she experiences nothing while doing it' and 'profound numbness' directly reflect emotional numbness

---

Rewrite the full vignette (4–5 paragraphs, third person) incorporating all missing items as lived clinical experience.
Preserve all content from the previous vignette that was already correct — only add what is missing.
Do not use section headers or bullet points.

# Clinical Vignette: Priya

Priya was twenty-one when the shelling came to her neighbourhood in Lahore. She had been visiting her grandmother for the summer before starting her final year of university, a trip she had made every year since childhood. Her grandmother's house sat on a quiet street lined with neem trees, three blocks from the main road. There was a moment of silence, then another blast—closer this time—and her grandmother grabbed her hand and pulled her toward the back room. Priya remembers this moment as a still image: her grandmother's face, the particular angle of afternoon light through the kitchen window, the feeling of her own hand being squeezed. Then another picture: crouching in the rear hallway, her grandmother's dupatta wrapped around both of them. Then nothing coherent—only fragments. A sound like breaking metal. The weight of her grandmother pressing against her. A smell she cannot name. A shape she saw but cannot quite hold in her mind, though it surfaces sometimes in her peripheral vision and makes her stomach clench. The shelling lasted perhaps twenty minutes, though Priya has no sense of time passing. When it stopped, there was dust in the air and a ringing in her ears that took hours to fade.

Now, two years later, Priya works as an auditor for a mid-sized firm in Chicago, where she moved to complete her degree and start her career. On the surface, her life appears orderly. She arrives at the office by eight-thirty, completes her spreadsheets with precision, and maintains cordial professional relationships with her colleagues. But something fundamental has shifted inside her, in a way she struggles to articulate even to herself. When she tries to explain to the intake clinician why she is here, the words scatter. She knows what happened—the event is not forgotten—but the experience itself feels locked behind glass. She can see it but cannot reach it, cannot translate it into language that makes sense. She has tried to write it down several times and abandoned the effort each time, frustrated and exhausted by the impossibility of finding the right words. When her supervisor asked her last month to document her whereabouts during a discrepancy in the quarterly audit, Priya found herself unable to construct a coherent written account of her own movements. The words would not come; the sequence of events dissolved into fragments the moment she tried to pin them down. She could see the moments—herself at her desk, herself in the break room—but could not weave them into narrative. Her supervisor noticed the incomplete report, and though nothing was said directly, Priya sensed the subtle shift in how she was regarded.

The triggers are specific and relentless. Two months ago, a colleague arrived at work on a bicycle, leaning it against the brick exterior of their building. When Priya saw the bicycle—the frame, the wheels, the way it stood upright in the morning sun—her heart began to race and she felt a sudden, overwhelming need to leave the office. She told her supervisor she was unwell and drove home, though she could not have explained why a bicycle frightened her. She knows, rationally, that bicycles have nothing to do with what happened. Yet the image of one is enough to send her into a state of hypervigilance that can last for hours. Similarly, any loud, percussive sound—a car backfiring, a door slamming, the sharp crack of a dropped file folder—sends her into immediate panic. She has begun to dread the commute to work, the unpredictability of urban noise, the sense that danger could announce itself at any moment. The bicycle incident marked a turning point. After that day, Priya began to avoid the office parking garage, taking surface streets instead, adding forty minutes to her commute. She stopped attending the firm's monthly all-hands meetings, where unexpected sounds from the building's heating system would trigger her panic. Within weeks, she had become the colleague who was "difficult to reach," who declined social invitations, who seemed withdrawn. Her performance reviews, which had been consistently strong, began to reflect a new concern: "Priya seems distracted and less engaged with team projects."

What troubles her most is the feeling that she is no longer herself. The person she was before that summer—competent, engaged, capable of imagining a future—feels like someone she used to know but has lost contact with. She sits in meetings and performs the role of auditor, but the performance feels hollow. She goes through the motions of her job with technical proficiency, yet she experiences nothing while doing it. No satisfaction, no frustration, no sense of accomplishment. It is as though she is watching herself from outside her body, observing her own hands moving across the keyboard, her own mouth forming words in meetings, but feeling nothing from within. When colleagues congratulate her on completing a complex audit, she hears the words but cannot access any pleasure or pride. She has come to believe that she is fundamentally broken, that something essential was taken from her during those minutes in her grandmother's hallway and has not returned. She describes herself as feeling "dead inside"—not suicidal, not actively wishing for death, but experiencing a profound numbness that makes her question whether she is still a person at all or merely an object moving through space, performing human functions without any of the interior aliveness that should accompany them. Her apartment has become a refuge, but even there she feels the absence of herself. She watches television without registering what she sees. She eats because she knows she must, not because food tastes like anything. She lies in bed at night and wonders if this shell—this functioning but hollow version of Priya—is all that remains.

It was her mother who finally insisted she seek help. During a video call last month, her mother noticed that Priya's voice sounded flat, her responses mechanical. When pressed, Priya admitted that she had been avoiding leaving her apartment on weekends, that she had declined her firm's invitation to a team lunch, that she could not remember the last time she had felt anything like joy or even mild pleasure. What frightened her most was the possibility that this numbness was permanent, that she would spend the rest of her life as a shell—functional but fundamentally absent from her own existence. She made the appointment with the clinician not out of hope, but out of a desperate need to understand whether the person she was is still somewhere inside her, or whether that person is truly gone.
